name: Knee Arthritis (Osteoarthritis)

seo_title: Knee Arthritis Treatment in North Palm Beach | First Rehab
seo_desc: Physical therapy for knee arthritis in North Palm Beach. One-on-one care to build strength, ease stiffness and keep you active. Medicare accepted.
lede: Knee arthritis can make stairs, walks and getting out of a chair harder, and exercise therapy is one of the best-supported ways to manage it.
what_it_is: Your knee is where the thighbone, shinbone and kneecap meet. The ends of those bones are covered with smooth articular cartilage, and a thin lining called the synovial membrane makes fluid that keeps the joint gliding. In osteoarthritis, the most common form of knee arthritis, the cartilage and other joint tissues gradually break down, so the knee becomes stiffer and more painful to use.

According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, osteoarthritis appears most often in people 50 and older, though younger adults can develop it, especially after a knee injury. NIAMS notes that women are more likely than men to have it, particularly after age 50. The American Physical Therapy Association reports that nearly 12.4 million Americans age 65 and older have symptomatic knee osteoarthritis.
symptoms: Aching pain with walking, stairs or standing up from a chair
Morning stiffness that usually eases within 30 minutes
Swelling or tenderness around the knee
Grinding, cracking or popping when you bend the knee
A sense that the knee is weak or might buckle
Trouble fully bending or straightening the leg
causes: Age, with most cases appearing after 50
Extra body weight, which adds load to the knee
A previous knee injury, such as a meniscus or ligament tear
Repetitive stress on the joint over many years
Low leg strength and activity level

how_therapy_helps.intro: The 2019 American College of Rheumatology and Arthritis Foundation guideline gives exercise a strong recommendation for knee osteoarthritis, along with weight loss for people who are overweight, self-management programs, tai chi and cane use. NIAMS notes that exercise can lower joint pain and stiffness while improving flexibility and muscle strength. Physical therapy turns that evidence into a structured plan: we find which muscles and motions are limiting you, then progress the work as your knee tolerates more.
methods: Exercises for the quadriceps, hamstrings and hips, the muscles that help absorb load for the knee. The American Physical Therapy Association notes that strengthening improves pain and quality of life in knee osteoarthritis.
Exercises and gentle stretching to keep the knee bending and straightening as fully as it can, which makes stairs, chairs and walking easier.
Hands-on joint mobilization and stretching, used alongside exercise to ease stiffness.
Practice standing and stepping on stable and less stable surfaces. The ACR guideline gives balance exercise a conditional recommendation for osteoarthritis.
Help swapping high-impact activities for lower-impact ones such as cycling or swimming, as the AAOS suggests, and pacing walks so you stay active with fewer flare-ups.
Advice on using a cane and whether a knee brace may help. The ACR guideline strongly recommends cane use and, for arthritis in the main knee joint, tibiofemoral bracing.

first_visit: Your therapist starts with how your knee affects your day: stairs, walking distance, getting up from low chairs. We then compare how far each knee bends and straightens, test strength in your thighs, hips and core, and watch you walk, squat and rise from sitting. We check for swelling and tenderness, ask about morning stiffness, and send you home with a starter exercise program.
recovery: Osteoarthritis is a long-term condition, so the goal of therapy is less pain and better function rather than a cure. How quickly you notice change depends on how long you have had symptoms, your activity level, other health conditions and how consistently you do your home program. Most plans involve a block of supervised visits followed by exercise you keep doing on your own. The ACR guideline encourages shared decision-making, so if conservative care is not enough, your doctor can talk with you about other options.
self_care: Stay active with low-impact exercise such as walking on level ground, cycling or swimming, and scale back if pain lingers into the next day
Use heat or ice for comfort, whichever feels better on your knee
Break up long periods of sitting so the knee does not stiffen
If you carry extra weight, gradual weight loss can lower the stress on your knee
Consider a cane on longer walks if the knee feels unsteady
see_a_doctor: Fever along with redness, warmth, pain and swelling in the knee (Mayo Clinic)
You cannot bear weight on the leg, or the knee gives out
You cannot fully straighten or bend the knee, or it locks
An obvious deformity of the knee or leg
Knee pain that does not improve within a few weeks (NHS)

faqs.q: Can physical therapy help knee arthritis?
faqs.a: Yes, for many people. The 2019 American College of Rheumatology and Arthritis Foundation guideline strongly recommends exercise for knee osteoarthritis, and the American Physical Therapy Association reports that strengthening improves pain and quality of life. A physical therapist designs and progresses that exercise for your knee, adds hands-on techniques and balance work, and teaches you how to keep active without repeated flare-ups.

faqs.q: Is walking good for arthritic knees?
faqs.a: Walking is usually a reasonable choice for knee osteoarthritis because it is low impact, and NIAMS notes that exercise can lower joint pain and stiffness. The key is dose. Start with distances that leave your knee no worse the next morning, use level ground and supportive shoes, and build gradually. If walking flares your knee, cycling or swimming can keep you moving while you build strength.

faqs.q: Should I rest my knee if I have arthritis?
faqs.a: Short breaks from activities that clearly aggravate the knee are fine, but long periods of rest tend to make osteoarthritis stiffer and weaker. NIAMS describes morning or after-rest stiffness as a common symptom, and exercise is the treatment the American College of Rheumatology recommends most strongly. Most people do best when they stay active within limits and adjust intensity rather than stopping altogether.

faqs.q: Does a knee brace help with arthritis?
faqs.a: It can for some people. The American College of Rheumatology guideline strongly recommends tibiofemoral bracing for arthritis in the main part of the knee joint, and conditionally recommends patellofemoral bracing when arthritis mainly affects the kneecap joint. The AAOS describes unloader braces that shift weight away from the worn side of the knee. A brace works best alongside exercise, and fit matters, so ask your therapist or doctor.

faqs.q: Does losing weight help knee arthritis?
faqs.a: For people who are overweight, yes. The American College of Rheumatology guideline strongly recommends weight loss for knee and hip osteoarthritis in that group, and NIAMS states that losing weight can help lower pain, prevent further injury and improve movement in the joints. The AAOS notes that weight loss reduces stress on the knee. Combining gradual weight loss with strengthening usually works better than either alone.

faqs.q: Is knee osteoarthritis the same as rheumatoid arthritis?
faqs.a: No. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons describes osteoarthritis as the degenerative, wear-and-tear form and the most common type of arthritis in the knee. Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune disease that attacks several joints throughout the body and is managed by a physician, often a rheumatologist, with specific medications. Physical therapy can help with strength and mobility in both, but the medical care differs.
